@graph.name: How to Hire a Senior Full Stack Developer — 7-Step Guide
@graph.description: A proven process for evaluating, interviewing, and onboarding a senior full stack developer for your product.

step.name: Define your tech stack requirements
step.text: Specify the frontend framework (React/Next.js), backend language (Python/Node.js), and any specific platform requirements (AWS, GCP, mobile). This narrows the candidate pool to developers with genuine expertise in your stack.

step.name: Review GitHub portfolio for production code
step.text: Request GitHub profile before any interview. Look for: multiple production projects (not tutorials), TypeScript usage, meaningful commit history over months, and real test coverage. Tutorial-clone repositories are a red flag.

step.name: Assess architecture depth, not syntax knowledge
step.text: Ask: 'How would you architect a multi-tenant SaaS database?' and 'How do you debug a slow API endpoint in production?' Senior developers discuss trade-offs and systematic approaches. Junior developers describe implementations.

step.name: Request a paid trial task
step.text: Pay $200–$500 for a small, well-defined task. Review the output for: code style consistency, error handling, input validation, test coverage, and documentation. The output reveals more than any interview.

step.name: Verify security practices
step.text: Ask how they handle: authentication (JWT best practices), input validation (Pydantic/Zod), SQL injection prevention (parameterized queries), and secrets management (environment variables, never Git). Non-answers indicate a security gap.

step.name: Establish milestone-based contract
step.text: Define specific deliverables at each milestone (not just 'start development'). Include acceptance criteria, payment schedule (30% deposit, 40% mid, 30% completion), IP ownership clause, bug warranty, and communication expectations.

step.name: Onboard with complete credential access
step.text: Provide: GitHub repository access, cloud platform access (read-only to start), all third-party API credentials, and a README or architecture overview. A good onboarding document saves 2–4 weeks of ramp-up time.

mainEntity.name: What is the tech stack a senior full stack developer uses in 2026?

acceptedAnswer.text: The production-proven 2026 full stack: Next.js 14 App Router with React Server Components, TypeScript strict mode, Tailwind CSS, React Query. Backend: FastAPI (Python) or NestJS (Node.js) with Pydantic v2, SQLAlchemy 2.0, Alembic migrations, Celery. Database: PostgreSQL 16, Redis, pgvector for AI embeddings. DevOps: Docker, GitHub Actions CI/CD, AWS or GCP, Nginx, Sentry, Prometheus + Grafana. AI layer: OpenAI GPT-4o or Claude 3.5 via API, LangChain, Pinecone or Qdrant, SSE streaming.

mainEntity.name: What security practices should a full stack developer implement by default?

acceptedAnswer.text: OWASP Top 10 compliance: (1) Parameterized queries — never string-formatted SQL. (2) JWT with 15-min access tokens, HTTP-only cookies for refresh tokens. (3) Server-side RBAC enforcement, row-level security in PostgreSQL. (4) Environment variables for all secrets. (5) CORS configured to specific origins, HSTS + CSP security headers. (6) bcrypt password hashing. (7) Rate limiting on auth endpoints. (8) GitHub Dependabot for dependency scanning. Security is built in from day one, not added later.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between hiring a full stack developer vs a software engineering team?

acceptedAnswer.text: Single senior full stack developer: $29/hr, direct communication, coherent architecture, fastest for MVP, limited concurrency. Best for pre-PMF startups and projects under $150K. Software engineering team: $15,000–$50,000+/month, coordination overhead, parallel feature development. Best for post-PMF products with validated market and series A+ funding. Most common mistake: hiring a team too early. Validate the product first with one excellent senior engineer.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if my existing full stack application needs a rewrite or just refactoring?

acceptedAnswer.text: Rewrite when: codebase is completely undocumented, every new feature requires touching 20+ files, technology is end-of-life, deployments are manual and risky. Refactor when: core logic is correct but messy, performance problems are localized, test coverage is poor but architecture is sound. Rule of thumb: if you can test-cover and refactor within 3 months without breaking production, refactor. Always start with a paid architecture audit ($599) before committing to either path.

mainEntity.name: How does a full stack developer implement WebSocket real-time features with FastAPI?

acceptedAnswer.text: FastAPI natively supports WebSockets. Architecture: (1) WebSocket endpoint handles connections and routing. (2) Connection manager maintains active connections per user. (3) Redis pub/sub distributes messages across multiple server instances for Kubernetes deployments. (4) Celery workers publish events to Redis when background tasks complete. For AI specifically: SSE (Server-Sent Events) is simpler than WebSockets for one-directional streaming — FastAPI's StreamingResponse with async generators handles this cleanly.
